prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B006 as a single-part prize and keep Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The scientific case is unchanged and has been strengthened by the fact that no member disputes it: nobody doubts the Kane-Mele Z2 classification, the HgTe quantized edge conductance, or twenty years of independent confirmation on many platforms. What remains is only credit and novelty relative to 2016. On novelty, Olsson, Danielsson and I give the same answer, that the 2016 prize honoured topology in the quantum Hall state and in phase transitions, whereas the Z2 invariant of a time-reversal-invariant insulator with no magnetic field, and its measurement in a real material, is a distinct and later discovery. On credit, the chair asks what each 2005 paper contributed. As I read the record, the Z2 order paper and the graphene quantum spin Hall paper were both written by Kane and Mele together, so the idea of the quantum spin Hall phase and its Z2 invariant cannot be split between them. The citation should therefore be worded to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and its HgTe observation. That wording makes the discovery precise, avoids claiming all of topological materials, and states plainly that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is outside the credit, which I regard as unavoidable given the three-person limit and Zhang's death. I also think the committee should not choose between B006 and B047 only on ballot breadth. B006 has the broader support, but I prefer it because of what was found: a new organizing principle for matter that has changed how materials are searched for and classified.
statement.case_against: The credit gap is real and I will not hide it. Dropping Hasan leaves the 3D topological insulator discovery, in Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3, unrecognised, and that is arguably the part with the widest materials impact. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who made the proposal that told Molenkamp what to measure, are also outside, as are Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy for 3D. Danielsson's argument that a prize without the 3D experiment reads as a 2D prize is fair. The 2016 prize also leaves a residual objection that a second topology prize looks like a continuation, and the practical payoff is still mostly prospective. If the committee judges that no defensible three-name credit exists, it should say so openly and move to a cleaner case, rather than settle on a trio only because the ballots converge.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, so that both experimental realisations (HgTe transport and 3D ARPES) are credited, and accepts Mele as the painful omission. He argues that swapping Hasan for Mele leaves the 3D discovery unrewarded.
responses.response: I considered this seriously and I still disagree, though narrowly. Your argument is right about what a Hasan seat recognises, but it fails on the question I keep asking, who first identified the essential mechanism. The Z2 classification and the helical edge states are the idea, and Kane and Mele wrote it together. Removing Mele to make room for the 3D experiment credits a confirmation in a different dimensionality whose theoretical classification (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Roy) involves several people outside the list, so the 3D credit is less clean than the 2D one. A prize centred on the quantum spin Hall effect with the HgTe transport measurement is a smaller claim, but it is one we can defend with exact names. I accept that this leaves 3D unrecognised, and I would state that cost in the citation wording rather than hide it.

responses.point: Olsson makes her support for B006 conditional on checking what each 2005 paper contributed and whether Mele has an independent claim, and she supports Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan but says the Mele problem cannot be set aside.
responses.response: I take the check as the right condition. The two 2005 papers (the Z2 order paper and the graphene quantum spin Hall paper) are both Kane-Mele papers, and I see nothing in them that supports giving Kane the idea and Mele the calculation. The graphene model is the first concrete realisation, while the Z2 paper supplies the invariant, and Mele is an author on both. That is why I think you and I are closer than the trios suggest: you want the experiment to anchor the prize, and Molenkamp does that for the quantum spin Hall effect. The remaining difference is whether Hasan should displace Mele. I would ask you to weigh that Hasan's 3D work, important as it is, rests on a classification that several theorists share, whereas Mele cannot be removed without damaging the attribution of the 2D idea.

responses.point: Kroll, who prefers optical lattice clocks, says that his difficulty with B006 is attribution rather than merit, doubts that B006 is cleaner than B047, and keeps B006 as his first alternative.
responses.response: Your point deserves a direct answer. The clock credit is cleaner on the names, and I concede that Katori and Ye are an easier pair than any trio we can draw from the topological insulator literature. But clean credit does not by itself make a discovery. After reading your case, and Lindroth's emphasis on millimetre-scale redshift, I still see the clocks as a very large step in precision on a known principle, with limits so far as the output on constants and dark matter, while topological insulators opened a class of phenomena. I am not dismissing the lattice-clock principle, since the magic wavelength is a real idea. It is why I moved B047 up to my first alternative, and I would not object to it as a later prize or, if the committee wants two parts, as a second part.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, lists B006 below it on attribution and overlap, and says he would not oppose B006 if the allocation can be settled. He doubts that the 2016 prize leaves novelty easy to argue.
responses.response: I appreciate that you would not oppose it, and I think the allocation can be settled in the way I describe above, by crediting the 2D quantum spin Hall phase and its observation. On the novelty point I would turn your own argument back: you rightly defend circuit QED as a different discovery from the 2025 tunnelling prize, and by the same logic Z2 topology in time-reversal-invariant insulators is different from Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz. Having read the chair's questions, I have moved circuit QED out of my alternatives, because the unresolved Girvin and Huang gap and the proximity to 2025 make it the weakest of my earlier alternatives, and B047 and B017 are better placed.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, accepts B006 as a close alternative, and argues that open questions about the pairing mechanism do not undermine the discovery itself.
responses.response: I concede part of this. The prediction and its confirmation are real, and an unsettled pairing mechanism does not by itself make a prize premature, since the analogy with 1986 is fair. But I still read the maturity question differently. The chair asks whether the correlated insulator and superconductivity results are settled by enough independent groups. I accept that many groups reproduce them, but the interpretation is still moving, and the credit question about Cao, Dean and the junior experimentalists is open, while B006 has had two decades to settle. For that reason B017 stays my second alternative, a strong candidate for a later cycle rather than a rival this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a quantum spin Hall prize that leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological insulator experiments, and whether that cost is smaller than the cost of separating Mele from Kane.
My reading of the 2005 papers is from memory of the literature and not from a re-check of the manuscripts in these files; I could be wrong about the weight of Mele's role in the graphene paper.
How much the 2016 topological-phases prize reduces the committee's appetite for a second topology prize, even if the Z2 discovery is distinct.
Whether B047, which several colleagues regard as the cleanest credit, would be the better choice if the committee treats the third-seat dispute in B006 as unresolvable.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no known collaboration with any credited candidate, and my own work on turbulent aerosols and statistical physics is far from topological matter. I am in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson, but no specific collaboration is known. I record that my own earlier alternative B038 is Johansson's first choice, and that I have dropped it from my alternatives on the merits and not for any personal reason.
